overview: “Catacomb culture” is an archaeological label, not the name of one state or people. It comes from shaft graves opening into side chambers, while excavated communities differed across the Dniester, Dnipro, Donets, Don, Manych, lower Volga, Crimea, and North Caucasus. The atlas draws one enormous polygon from 2000 to 1500 BCE. Its 2000 BCE outline includes Chisinau, Odesa, Crimea, Rostov, Volgograd, Astrakhan, Atyrau, the North Caucasus, and Baku probes, an extent no excavation map should be mistaken for a surveyed frontier. Regional radiocarbon studies commonly place Catacomb traditions earlier, mainly in the later third millennium BCE, with endings and post-Catacomb formations varying by place. Burials dominate the evidence, but seasonal camps reveal herding, pottery repair, metalworking, fishing, plant use, and repeated movement through river valleys and grasslands. Graves preserve children, women, men, ornaments, wagons, injuries, and careful construction, yet they are not household censuses. No securely attributed Catacomb writing survives, so no invented language sample appears here. The 1500 BCE repaint to “Cimerians” is a software seam, centuries too early to name a successor.

periods.title: 2000 to 1938 BCE: the atlas catches a late horizon
periods.summary: The exact polygon appears only in the 2000 BCE snapshot. Regional dates place East Manych Catacomb graves mainly around 2500 to 2300 BCE, with mixed and polyritual contexts extending toward 2200 BCE. This first view therefore represents late and uneven survivals, not the beginning of one culture.

periods.title: 1938 to 1875 BCE: one polygon hides many chronologies
periods.summary: Catacomb chronologies depend on region, grave type, material associations, and sample quality. Human bone dates in the North-West Caspian can appear too old when diets included river and lake foods. A neat atlas interval cannot replace paired dates, local sequences, and reservoir corrections.

periods.title: 1875 to 1813 BCE: post-Catacomb formations already matter
periods.summary: Around 2200 cal BCE, the Lola cultural circle and other post-Catacomb formations emerged in parts of the Volga-Manych and Caucasian steppe. Archaeological and biological connections vary locally. By this atlas slice, calling the entire polygon simply Catacomb obscures active transformation.

periods.title: 1813 to 1750 BCE: regional paths diverge
periods.summary: The Volga-Ural post-Catacomb group is dated around 2200 to 2000 cal BCE and belongs to a broader field of changing traditions. It cannot stand for the Dnipro, Donets, Crimea, or Caucasus. Different local endings rule out one empire-style fall narrative.

periods.title: 1750 to 1688 BCE: people continue beyond labels
periods.summary: Genome-wide evidence shows long stability among steppe pastoral populations during peak Early and Middle Bronze Age expansion, followed later by complex gene flow and transformation. Archaeological labels changed without making families vanish. Genetic continuity also cannot identify a language, tribe, or political border.

periods.title: 1688 to 1625 BCE: later evidence is not one sequel
periods.summary: North Caucasus research identifies a post-Catacomb horizon around 2200 to 1700 cal BCE with more than one ancestry profile and several archaeological labels. That diversity undercuts a single successor arrow. It also shows why the atlas’s southern extension needs regional caution.

periods.title: 1625 to 1563 BCE: the imported outline outlasts consensus
periods.summary: The atlas still paints the target across Ukraine, southern Russia, Kazakhstan, Crimea, the North Caucasus, and Azerbaijan. Published regional studies do not support one Catacomb institution spanning that whole late interval. Map coverage continues here; the researched archaeological chronology does not.

periods.title: 1563 to 1500 BCE: an anachronistic repaint approaches
periods.summary: At 1500 BCE the target disappears and nearly every sampled interior point becomes “Cimerians”; Atyrau becomes Karasuk. Those labels persist at 1000 BCE, then change again at 700 BCE. The synchronized repaint is cartographic, not evidence for conquest, migration, or a named successor.

sections.title: Read the exact map before naming its people

items.text: The index has one exact catacomb-culture record: a circa archaeological culture with map coverage from 2000 to 1500 BCE. It has one border file, no researched card, and no override. This packet applies only to that id, because similar burial labels elsewhere require their own identity checks.

The sole feature is one polygon with one ring and 219 positions. Its bounds run from about 24.29 to 53.18 degrees east and 39.97 to 49.36 degrees north. That measurement describes imported software geometry, not a Bronze Age survey, treaty line, or shared government.

Seventeen probes test inside: Chisinau, Odesa, Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk, Mariupol, Rostov, Volgograd, Elista, Astrakhan, Atyrau, Crimea, Krasnodar, Stavropol, Nalchik, Makhachkala, and Baku. Kyiv, Kharkiv, Saratov, Oral, Tbilisi, and Yerevan test outside. Points audit geometry; they do not assign ancient identities.

At 3000 BCE, most future target probes are painted Yamnaya. At 2000 BCE they change together to Catacomb culture. Archaeology finds overlap and regional development, so the atlas seam cannot establish population replacement. Prehistoric border clerks have not, despite excellent preservation conditions in spreadsheets, appeared in any grave.

The imported summary gives 2500 to 1950 BCE, while the geometry gives 2000 to 1500 BCE. Neither range is universal across every regional group. The card keeps map coverage in metadata, explains archaeological dates in prose, and leaves fell null rather than disguising a snapshot endpoint as history.

sections.title: Build chronology from regions, dates, and contexts

items.text: Kalmyk Catacomb chronology changed when researchers calibrated radiocarbon evidence and compared archaeological sequences. Regional development cannot be dated by transferring one grave’s age across the whole Pontic-Caspian steppe. A date belongs with its sample, material, laboratory method, and local cultural assignment.

North-West Caspian researchers paired human and herbivore bones because aquatic foods can produce a reservoir effect in human collagen. Fish and mollusks were historically interesting twice over: they fed people, and they complicated the clock archaeologists use to date them.

The Ingul-Dnieper and Donets traditions differ in grave construction, pottery, distribution, and research history. Calling them one culture can help comparison, but it must not erase local sequences. “Catacomb” is therefore best read as a cultural-historical umbrella whose internal boundaries remain analytical, not governmental.

Middle Dniester Catacomb graves extend the phenomenon westward, but their construction and chronology require local analysis. At studied barrows, the absence of later graves cutting earlier ones suggests visible markers above some burials. That observation supports remembered places, not a centralized cemetery authority.

Clay censers vary in form and ornament across eastern steppe contexts, and scholars have repeatedly revised their relative chronology. They are useful comparison tools, but an object type does not carry a passport. Similarity can reflect contact, imitation, movement, or shared practice.

sections.title: Follow homes, camps, herds, and seasons

items.text: Lower Don camps at Volochaika and Chikalda were occupied in summer and early autumn. Fragmented everyday pots were made or replaced during those stays, while ritual vessels in kurgans often matched clays from farther away. Mobile life included repair decisions, not simply endless wandering.

At Ksizovo-1, sequential carbon, oxygen, and strontium measurements from cattle and sheep or goat teeth indicate year-round C3 forage and mostly local ecological ranges. Herd movement was small-scale there. One forest-steppe settlement therefore corrects the stereotype that every pastoral household crossed continents.

Kalmyk pastoralists used river valleys, upland plateaux, and open grasslands at different seasons. Movement balanced water, pasture, and herd needs across a dry landscape. This was organized ecological work, although routes and distances varied and cannot be copied unchanged onto the entire atlas polygon.

Middle Don settlement placement suggests winter shelters on lower floodlands and terraces, with summer camps on higher promontories and terraces above seasonal floods. Cattle were prominent. The pattern joins landscape, herd needs, and season, while remaining specific to the studied forest-steppe region.

Rykan-3 preserved a single Middle Don Catacomb layer that researchers model as a winter cattle-breeding settlement. A single layer can clarify one season precisely, yet it cannot supply the floor plan of every household from Moldova to the Caspian. Archaeological honesty sometimes travels lighter than a wagon.

sections.title: Eat, drink, fish, and manage animals

items.text: Human and animal isotope results from southern Russian steppe and piedmont sites show diets varied by location and ecology. Catacomb-associated graves at Rasshevatskiy and Marinskaya belong within long mound histories containing several cultures. Their food signals are local biographies, not a universal Catacomb menu.

Crusts inside East and West Manych funerary vessels contained wild-steppe plant traces and barley phytoliths. One directly dated sample connected barley parts with ritual, but researchers found no proof that local Lower Don pastoralists farmed it. Grain could arrive through exchange or seasonal travel.

North-West Caspian stable isotopes, vessel residues, stomach contents, and fish remains point to substantial use of rivers and lakes. Pike, sturgeon, carp, mollusks, and water plants broaden the picture beyond meat and milk. Aquatic foods also explain why some human radiocarbon dates need correction.

At Ksizovo-1, cattle and sheep or goat tooth sequences suggest people influenced calving and lambing seasons. Managing birth timing requires observation, feed planning, and coordinated labor. The study supports skilled husbandry in one Middle Don community without claiming a standardized herding calendar everywhere.

Southern Russian steppe sites show livestock, fish, plant foods, and exchanged goods within mixed economies shaped by local ecology. Isotopes and residues make movement look like seasonal adaptation rather than aimless roaming. Dinner depended on landscapes and connections, not a single heroic steak or one universal menu.

sections.title: Make pottery, tools, ornaments, and metal

items.text: Portable X-ray fluorescence and technological study found that everyday ceramics at Lower Don temporary camps used nearby materials and were replaced as needed. Kurgan vessels often came from other production zones. Ordinary pots therefore reveal movement, curation, and separate ritual choices more clearly than grand labels do.

At Ksizovo-1, smelting and casting tools provide direct evidence for copper and bronze work at a settlement, not only finished objects placed in graves. Comparable Don forest-steppe finds show that metal production occurred within lived landscapes, although workshop scale and specialist status remain debated.

Forged copper and bronze plates, beads, and hoops occur on burial garments in different arrangements. Ingul graves especially preserve small plate ornaments. Placement helps reconstruct clothing and display, but grave costume cannot automatically become everyone’s daily outfit or a fixed gender uniform.

Northern Eurasian metallurgical research records Catacomb knives and other copper-alloy objects, yet ore sources and production are unevenly studied. Similar forms found far apart can mark exchange, travelling craft knowledge, or local copying. They do not prove one workshop controlled the steppe.

Flint manufacture remained important beside bronze. Tool kits from burial complexes preserve selected implements and production traces, showing skilled stoneworking continued in the Middle Bronze Age. Because graves are curated deposits, archaeologists must not mistake every buried kit for a complete working inventory.

sections.title: Read burials without turning them into a census

items.text: The defining grave often has an entrance shaft, a passage or step, and a side chamber beneath a mound. Construction demanded planning and group labor. Regional designs vary, and the name describes archaeology rather than underground towns, secret empires, or the much later Roman catacombs.

At Revova Kurgan 3, dated phases show repeated use of one North Pontic mound across generations and archaeological traditions. Such reuse made mounds durable places of memory. It does not mean every later burial belonged to the same family, language, or political institution.

Two East Manych men from the Ergeninskii kurgan group shared a paternal lineage category but had different maternal lineages. The sample is too small to define Catacomb kinship. DNA can test biological relationships; it cannot by itself recover adoption, alliance, affection, or household membership.

Wagons or wheel parts sometimes lay in entrance shafts rather than burial chambers. Their placement was a ritual choice as well as evidence of transport technology. Exceptional wagon graves cannot show that every family owned a vehicle, any more than one parked limousine describes an entire modern neighborhood.

Differences in mound position, chamber construction, and grave goods have supported competing models of hierarchy and pastoral organization. Weapons can signify power without proving a warrior class or constant warfare. Burial treatment records social decisions about the dead, not a transparent spreadsheet of the living.

sections.title: See families, children, women, and learning

items.text: A Kalmyk Scientific Center review found that sampled children’s Catacomb burials broadly shared adult grave structures and accompanying objects. Children were recognized in mortuary practice, but cemetery selection remains unknown. The evidence cannot tell whether every child received burial or how childhood stages were named.

Some women’s Ingul Catacomb graves contained weapons. Those discoveries challenge a simple rule assigning all arms to men, yet they do not prove identical roles for all women or that every weapon marks combat. Sex estimates, object context, age, and regional chronology must stay together.

Multiple burials and repeated mound use can preserve biological relatives, social partners, or people joined by ritual. Ancient DNA tests consanguinity where preservation allows, while grave arrangement shows chosen commemoration. Family life included relationships that neither genes nor objects can fully name.

No schoolroom, lesson text, or named teacher is securely attributed to these communities. Children still had to learn animals, seasons, pottery, fibers, fire, routes, and grave customs. The responsible inference is learning through participation and instruction, without inventing a classroom schedule or universal initiation ceremony.

Seasonal settlement decisions required people to coordinate shelter, herd care, food storage, tool repair, and movement. Younger members could observe and practice these tasks, but exact ages and divisions are unknown. Potsherds survive more readily than bedtime advice, a bias the card keeps visible.

sections.title: Treat health, injury, bodies, and care cautiously

items.text: A man aged about 45 to 50 from an Inhul Catacomb grave near Novoivanivka had a healed depressed cranial injury and evidence interpreted as surgical treatment. Healing proves survival after trauma; one case does not establish a profession, standard procedure, anaesthetic, or regional medical system.

An East Manych woman from the North Caucasus had cemento-osseous dysplasia, a rare jaw condition identified through modern imaging and differential diagnosis. The finding extends the condition’s known history. It does not show that Bronze Age caregivers named it, recognized its cause, or treated it.

X-ray study of intentionally shaped Low Volga skulls also recorded trauma and ear disease. Intentional head shaping was a cultural practice, not itself an illness. Researchers must separate chosen bodily modification, injury, disease, and postmortem change before discussing health or social identity.

Two male skeletons from the Sugokleya barrow preserve cranial injuries and occupational stress markers, one associated with an Ingul Catacomb burial. Such bones reveal episodes and repeated strain, not the exact work that caused each mark. A skeleton records consequences more readily than caregiving.

Pregnancy, birth, fever, wounds, disability, aging, and grief required care, but no reviewed source supplies a Catacomb remedy list, dosage, healer’s kit, or medical text. Healed injury demonstrates survival and likely assistance; it cannot identify who helped, which treatment mattered, or what people believed.

sections.title: Find water, waste, sanitation, and toilets honestly

items.text: Seasonal camps clustered near water and shifted between floodlands and higher terraces. That placement gave access to people and herds while avoiding some spring flooding. It is settlement planning at a landscape scale, but it does not reveal drinking-water treatment, containers, assigned watering turns, or purity rules.

Rykan-3 offers a winter settlement layer with subsistence evidence, yet its published reconstruction does not securely identify a latrine, sewer, drain, or toilet structure. Absence in the report is not proof that residents ignored waste. It defines what this card may safely claim.

Temporary camps produced broken pottery, hearth debris, animal waste, food remains, and worn tools, but reviewed studies focus on seasonality and production rather than mapped refuse rules. Cleaning and disposal certainly happened somehow. Their locations, tools, privacy customs, and household responsibilities remain undocumented.

Toilet verdict: no reviewed Catacomb settlement publication securely identifies a privy, toilet seat, cesspit, sewer, fecal deposit, or written sanitation rule. People relieved themselves; archaeology has not supplied the arrangement. No palace plumbing is unsurprising, but no evidence is not permission to invent a bush.

Dwellings and camps are much less studied than kurgans, so daily maintenance is underrepresented before excavation even begins. Burial architecture can survive dramatically while swept surfaces, dung handling, bedding, washing, and temporary screens disappear. The evidence is lopsided; hygiene should not be judged by the most durable holes.

sections.title: Keep language, achievements, and endings evidence bound

items.text: Written-language sample: none securely known. Original script: not applicable. Transliteration: not applicable. Translation: not applicable. Date and attribution: Catacomb-associated regional communities, mainly later third millennium BCE. Reviewed graves, camps, pots, tools, bodies, and ornaments preserve no demonstrated target inscription, so assigning readable words or a specific language would fabricate evidence.

Complex side-chamber graves, seasonal herding, managed animal births, local pottery replacement, copper casting, flint craft, wagons, and long exchange routes are real achievements visible in different regions. The achievement is accumulated practical knowledge, not an invented first, one capital, or one ruler claiming credit.

Genome-wide studies find Catacomb-associated steppe individuals within broader patterns of long-term stability and regional contact. Genes illuminate ancestry and movement; they cannot name speech, religion, ethnicity, or political membership. A pottery label and a genetic cluster answer different questions even when they overlap.

Around 2200 cal BCE, Lola and other post-Catacomb formations appear in parts of the Volga-Manych and Caucasian steppe. Links include continuity, movement, and new combinations rather than one clean replacement. Other western and northern regions followed different sequences, so no single successor id is safe.

The atlas ends this id at 1500 BCE by repainting most probes “Cimerians” and Atyrau “Karasuk.” That is hundreds of years after many regional transformations and cannot document a conquest. The exact record therefore ends as a map layer, while communities and practices continued through locally named archaeological histories.

ending.text: Catacomb traditions did not collapse as one state. Regional chronologies place East Manych and several related groups largely in the later third millennium BCE, while Lola and other post-Catacomb formations developed around 2200 to 2000 cal BCE in some eastern zones and different sequences unfolded farther west. The imported 1950 BCE endpoint is only a broad conventional marker; the atlas continues the exact polygon to 1500 BCE, then repaints nearly all tested locations “Cimerians” and one “Karasuk.” No reviewed source supports that synchronized succession. Families, herding knowledge, craft traditions, routes, and mound places continued through changing local communities. The override keeps 2000 to 1500 BCE as map coverage, sets fell to null, and names no predecessor or successor.
